cross_cutting_findings.text: Benchmark artefacts change conclusions in KG completion. Test leakage through inverse relations is reported for FB15k and WN18 [S24, K19-2]; FB15k-237 remains partly solvable by a non-learning frequency baseline, with less than five points of embedding gain on about 40% of its test triples [S16]; and tie-handling in ranking inflated the reported performance of several neural models, compounded by a test-leakage bug in one implementation [S03]. Biomedical KGs show the same leakage risk through reciprocal ISA relations [S10].

Several widely used benchmarks are biased toward easy cases. Entity-alignment benchmarks DBP15K and WK3L have degree distributions far denser than their source KGs [S05]; GrailQA's zero-shot split is over 97% simple isomorphism classes [S23]; the BetaE complex-query data covers few complex query types [S13]; and fairness datasets built from tabular data with similarity edges give the graph no informative structure [S07, S12].

KGQA benchmarks carry substantial label error. A manual audit of 15 KGQA datasets (16 counting LC-QuAD 1.0 and 2.0 separately) found 52% of sampled WebQSP items and 49.33% of sampled CWQ items factually correct, with GrailQA at 30% and MetaQA at 20% on 60-item samples [S20]. Gold answers also drift as the underlying KG changes, which CBench addresses by re-querying the endpoint [S15]. Both papers point to executable, re-verifiable queries as a remedy [S15, S20].

Benchmark design is shifting toward LLM-centred KG engineering. New resources evaluate LLMs on mapping generation [S09, S11], Turtle repair and KG generation [S19], text-to-Cypher over provenance-rich KGs [S08], SPARQL-verified multi-hop QA [S20], dialogue benchmark generation [S21] and KG-grounded factuality [S22]. Common reported constraints are context-window limits forcing task decomposition [S09], ontology leakage into model training data [S11], and dependence on the accuracy of the source KG [S20].

Downstream value of completion is not equal to completion accuracy. The best KG completion model does not yield the best QA accuracy on CompleQA [S17]; provenance-aware embeddings give negligible single-city gains on AuthentiCity [S08]; and BOW features mostly outperform KG embeddings for malware detection [S18].

Domain and enterprise KGs are often closed or semi-synthetic. Unreleased or restricted resources include the AliMe knowledge base [K19-12], ECKG [S22], the CCKS 2018 clinical NER data (data-use agreement) [K19-14] and the Telkomsel HR graph [S14]. Semi-synthetic generation appears in the Industry 4.0 dataset (randomised sensor values) [S04], MEED (model-generated text) [K21-23] and the synthetic fairness graphs [S07].

Version and provenance reporting is inconsistent. Many rows carry an RI note that the dump date or version is missing (for example K19-1, K19-4, K19-13, K21-5), and one paper labels a WN18RR-sized graph as WN11 [S25]. This supports a recommendation that the survey's taxonomy record dataset version as a required attribute.

Gaps. No dataset use in this batch addresses KG-to-text generation or KG maintenance and evolution directly; the closest evidence is yearly cumulative patent KGs used for link and patent prediction [K21-17] and answer drift handling in CBench [S15].

Redundancy in link-prediction benchmarks is quantified beyond inverse relations. Akrami et al. report that about 70% of FB15k test triples have reverse triples in training, 142 of 1,345 FB15k relations are Cartesian-product relations, and two near-duplicate YAGO3-10 relations cover over 63% of its test set; they release YAGO3-10-DR [B01]. This extends the Batch 1 evidence on FB15k/WN18 leakage and FB15k-237 shortcuts. Pattern-specific splits of FB15K and WN18 [B16] and rule-controlled continual benchmarks from FB15k-237 [B21] show the same datasets being re-purposed rather than replaced.

Reference datasets themselves need quality assessment. Rule-based curation of GERBIL NER/EL datasets found systematic annotation errors and up to 10% micro-F changes when tools were re-scored [E17-19]; KGQA datasets mostly cannot test compositional or zero-shot generalisation [B13]; and sampling-based estimation makes KG accuracy auditing affordable (e.g., MOVIE estimated at 88% $$ 5% from 174 annotated triples) [B09].

Resource papers dominate the semantic-web volumes. ISWC 2019 Resources and In-Use chapters introduce domain KGs (ArCo, MAKG, FoodKG, SEPSES, SemanGit, ClaimsKG, YAGO2geo) and crawls (BTC-2019), while standalone papers add VulKG, PKG, PharmKG, CSKG, ASER, I40KG and Otter-Knowledge [I19-3, I19-8, I19-10, I19-13, I19-14, I19-20, I19-12, I19-11, B02, B07, B19, B08, B05, B06, B17]. Evaluation of these resources is mostly descriptive (statistics, competency questions, example queries) rather than measured accuracy, with exceptions such as matching precision in YAGO2geo [I19-12] and disambiguation validation in PKG [B07].

KGs are increasingly used as instruments to evaluate LLMs. GraphEval builds KGs from LLM outputs to detect hallucinations [B10]; MultiHal pairs hallucination benchmarks with Wikidata paths in several languages [B15]; Semantic-KG perturbs KG subgraphs to test semantic-similarity judges [B23]; BRINK removes supporting triples to test KG-RAG under incompleteness [B25]. Reported constraints include machine-translation quality for low-resource languages [B15] and sensitivity to perturbation type [B23].

Systems benchmarks rely on synthetic or ageing data. Storage and query papers use BSBM, LUBM and WatDiv [I19-15, I19-17, I19-19, E17-37], synthetic streams [E17-14], or regional OSM/SSURGO extracts [B18]; the Batch 1 Wikidata 2016 dump study is of the same kind.

Category coverage changes. This batch supplies the first evidence for KG maintenance and evolution (continual KGE benchmarks [B21]) and adds substantial evidence for quality assessment (16 rows). KG-to-text generation still has no direct evidence.

New benchmarks are justified by audits of existing ones. Galkin et al. report that about 44.5% of JF17K test statements share their main triple with training statements and that fewer than 3% of WikiPeople facts are hyper-relational; they release WD50K and three qualifier-ratio subsets from a 2019 Wikidata dump, with test leakage removed by construction [C19]. Kotnis et al. state that no existing dataset contained conjunctive queries with multiple missing entities and derive FB15K-237-CQ and WN18RR-CQ [C01]. Both continue the Batch 1 and 2 pattern of re-purposing FB15k-237 and WN18RR rather than replacing them.

KG-enhanced LLM evaluation splits into two benchmark lines. Freebase-based KGQA uses WebQSP, CWQ and GrailQA with Exact Match [C04]; multiple-choice QA uses CommonsenseQA and OpenBookQA with ConceptNet, and MedQA-USMLE with UMLS-derived KGs [C13, C21]. Medical dialogue QA relies on KGs built by the authors and on BERTScore and GPT-4 judgements rather than human raters [C20]. KnowGPT names noisy triples in automatically constructed KGs as its main limitation [C21].

Freebase is still the most reused backbone. Five papers use it as the QA KG, the entity-linking target, the source of item knowledge or the source of entity descriptions [C04, C06, C07, C15, C22], although none discusses its discontinuation. ConceptNet, UMLS, FB15k-237, WN18RR and Wikidata follow with three papers each.

Recommendation KGs are attached by the authors. DiffKG maps Last-FM items to Freebase, collects a Wikidata KG for MIND and builds a category KG for Alibaba-iFashion [C15]; Relphormer adds Freebase descriptions to ML-20m [C22]. Reported results therefore depend on mapping choices that are not benchmarks in their own right.

Construction and application papers often lack quantitative evaluation. AutoKG found a WikiWhy comparison uninformative and reports qualitative cases [C09]; the e-learning DSKG, university-courses KG, LifeGraph and GTKG papers report no task-level evaluation [C12, C14, C18, C25]. Where evaluation exists it is often very small: one expert [C02], one student evaluator [C06], one validation term [C10].

Category coverage. This batch adds evidence for KG maintenance and evolution through automatic expansion of ConceptNet [C10] and for quality refinement through the GTKG lifecycle example [C25]. It contains no direct evidence for ontology and typing, entity resolution, KG-to-text generation, or the four categories added in Batch 1. Text-to-SQL over a schema KG [C16] is placed under KG question answering; this placement is a reviewer decision.

Recommendation KGs form a reuse chain built by name matching. KGAT releases KG versions of Amazon-book, Last-FM and Yelp2018, mapping items to Freebase by title matching (with two-hop triplets) or using Yelp's local business network [D11]; JNSKR reuses Amazon-book and Yelp2018 and states they are exactly the same as in KGAT, with identical statistics [D09]. KGCN builds Microsoft Satori sub-KGs for MovieLens-20M, Book-Crossing and Last.FM and excludes items with multiple or no matched entities [D14]; MaORS-KGE builds its own KG from a MovieLens10M extension [D03]. None of these papers reports the accuracy of the item-to-entity alignment (RI).

LLM-era KG construction is mostly checked by automatic references or LLM judges. Generated book and landmark KGs are scored by exact match against Wikidata, which the authors call strict, with a manual check of 180 unmatched relations [D05]; KARMA's enrichment is judged by LLM-based metrics, which its authors list as a limitation [D10]; FactFinder uses an LLM-as-a-judge on 69 questions [D04]. The one controlled comparison uses 3.6K expert-labelled CS-KG triples: LLM validation raises precision from 75% to 87%, while fully manual and fully automated workflows trade precision against recall [D20].

Small, author-built domain KGs serve as priors for non-KG benchmarks. The Chemical Element KG (1,643 triples) and ElementKG guide molecular pre-training on ZINC15 and fine-tuning on MoleculeNet [D25, D21]; SpaTalk assembles a ligand–receptor–TF KG from CellTalkDB, KEGG, Reactome and AnimalTFDB [D22]; PrimeKG is reused as a retrieval source for biomedical QA and diagnosis prediction [D04, D07]. In these papers the downstream datasets contain no KG, so the KG is evaluated only through task performance (RI).

The 2013 Semantic Web volume rests on DBpedia, ontology repositories and synthetic benchmarks. DBpedia is the most reused family in the batch (see the table above). Ontology studies draw on BioPortal, TONES and the Oxford library [I13-3, I13-6, I13-13, I13-21, I13-28], and Matentzoglu et al.\ warn that results may be biased, even heavily, towards such hand-curated corpora before building a crawl-based OWL corpus [I13-21]. Query-processing and reasoning chapters rely on LUBM and BSBM, often modified by the authors because the original LUBM TBox lacks existential restrictions and depth [I13-20, I13-27, I13-35, I13-41, I13-45, I13-16].

Energy-domain KG evidence is qualitative. Fensel et al.\ describe Wien Energie and Energienetze Steiermark KGs that drive customer chatbots, but report no data release or evaluation [D08]. For FlexPED this is a use case, not a reusable dataset.

Category coverage. This batch adds most evidence to KG-supported applications, ontology/schema and typing, and KG construction. KG question answering, KG-to-text generation and KG maintenance each have one paper [D04, D18, D10]; there is no evidence for fairness and bias or KG-grounded evaluation of LLMs. Placements of licence analysis under quality assessment [I13-10] and of infobox link discovery under KG completion [I13-42] are reviewer decisions.

Surveys supply catalogues, not evidence of use. Seventeen of the 23 standalone files are surveys or reviews. None runs its own experiments; result tables are compiled from the original papers (F03, PDF p. 19; F08, PDF pp. 23 and 25). Their dataset catalogues (e.g., 49 static, 18 temporal and 11 multi-modal KG reasoning datasets in F16; Tables 6–8 of F03; MMKG statistics in F11) are recorded in Section as candidates for follow-up rather than as rows.

Resource papers introduce KGs and ontologies but rarely evaluate them quantitatively. Of the 23 ISWC 2018 chapters, ontology and vocabulary resources (Audio Commons, HeLiS, Drammar, SPAR, CSO, VoCaLS, cancer staging terms) report expert assessment, uptake or application-based evidence rather than benchmark results [I18-2, I18-4, I18-7, I18-8, I18-12, I18-14, I18-16]. The GeoLink complex-alignment benchmark is released without running any alignment system on it [I18-17].

Recommendation KGs are author-built subsets. RippleNet selects Satori triples with movie or book relations and confidence above 0.9 and expands up to four hops [F20]; KTUP maps items to DBpedia following LODRecSys, filters low-frequency entities and merges relations manually, with only 19.95% and 18.25% of entities aligned to items [F24]. This repeats the Batch 3 observation that recommendation results depend on mapping choices that are not benchmarks in their own right.

Temporal KG completion benchmarks are re-derived after audits. Time2Box reports that 56.2% of temporal statements in its Wikidata sample lack validity information, that WIKIDATA12k excludes such statements, and that WIKIDATA432k contains date errors (e.g., 2014 written as 2401), and builds the corrected WIKIDATA114k subgraph [F22].

Evaluation sets are often very small. T2KG uses 100 manually annotated sentences [F21]; VoxEL has 15 articles per language [I18-11]; the cancer-staging study re-stages 250 SEER records [I18-14]; MINTE+ reports 85% accuracy on 100 molecules [I18-22]; Smart Book Recommender is evaluated by 14 people [I18-21].

DBpedia is the most reused backbone in this batch. Eight papers use it, as the target KG for text-to-KG mapping [F21], the item KG for recommendation [F24], the KB behind KBQA linking benchmarks [W19-3], a mapping target for topics [I18-5, I18-12], a query-performance workload [I18-6, I18-13] and an integration source [I18-22].

Category coverage and placement decisions. This batch adds evidence for ontology and schema resources (C2), KG integration and alignment (C3) and storage and query processing (C13). It contains no main-table evidence for KG reasoning, KG-to-text generation, KG retrieval and search, KG maintenance and evolution, fairness and bias, or KG-grounded evaluation of LLMs. Reviewer decisions: multilingual entity linking (VoxEL) is placed under C1 and KBQA entity/relation linking (EEARL) under C6; complex ontology alignment (GeoLink) and medical-source integration (Babylon LDG) under C3; LODAtlas under C14; the community-detection chapter W19-4 is placed in the peripheral table because its networks are homogeneous co-authorship and hyperlink graphs, despite the authors' KG framing.

Surveys rarely re-run experiments. Of 25 surveys, only G04 trains and tests models itself, on FB15k and FB15k-237 in one environment, and it names its two-dataset scope as a limitation (p. 22). Results tables in G02, G12 and G22 are explicitly compiled from published papers or leaderboards; G22 omits leaderboard scores that "lack clear sources" (p. 11).

The same benchmark name carries different statistics across surveys. WN18RR is given 40,943 entities [G02, PDF p. 2], 40,953 [G11, p. 12] and 40,493 [G15, p. 99]; G11 attributes it to Bordes et al.\ (2014), G15 to Dettmers et al.\ (2018). ICEWS14 has 6,869 entities in G09 (Table 1, p. 3) and 7,128 in G10 (Table 1, p. 5) and G17 (Table 2, p. 4); ICEWS05-15 has 461,329 facts in G10 and 479,329 in G17. GDELT appears with 500 entities and 20 relations [G09 interpolation setting; G17] and with 7,691 entities and 240 relations [G09 extrapolation setting; G10], and the 500-entity version has 24-hour granularity in G09 but 15-minute granularity in G17. ComplexQuestions has 2,100 questions in G22 (Table 5, p. 11) and 150 in G25 (Table A1, p. 23). G01 gives Wikidata5M 1,222 relations in Table 3 but 822 in the text (p. 21). Statistics for the final paper should therefore be taken from the original dataset releases, not from surveys.

Known benchmark defects recur. Inverse-relation leakage in FB15k and WN18 motivated FB15k-237 and WN18RR [G02, PDF p. 2; G15, p. 98]; KB-GAT results carry an evaluation-protocol error and test leakage [G02, PDF p. 8]. G06 reports that re-weighting evaluation to remove degree and relation-frequency bias lowers reported KGEM performance on FB15k and YAGO3-10 (PDF p. 4). G25 notes the rigid templates of SimpleQuestions (p. 19). Freebase is described as deprecated or discontinued yet still widely used [G22, p. 10; G25, p. 19], and no Wikidata or DBpedia analogue of FB2M/FB5M is known [G25, p. 19].

Surveys name explicit benchmark gaps. No accessible KG-evolution dataset combines fact labels with time, and none supplies explanations [G15, p. 106]; there is a shortage of systematic benchmarks for the long-term reliability of KG agents [G16, p. 27]; harmonisation of automotive ontologies and driving-dataset structures is needed before KG use [G07, PDF p. 11]; smart-city KG data still focus on small scopes such as traffic and flood events [G05, p. 223:8].

Domain catalogues for the taxonomy. Batch 6 supplies structured inventories of domain resources: 37 biomedical databases and ontologies and 31 biomedical KGs with statistics [G23]; cybersecurity sources CVE, CWE, CAPEC, CPE, NVD and ATT&CK [G14]; educational KGs such as MOOCCube KG and CKGG [G18]; urban KGs Km4City, Sii-Mobility and UrbanKG, with energy management as a named subdomain [G05]; open multimodal KGs MMKG, IMGpedia, Richpedia, ImageGraph and VisualSem [G08]; entity-alignment benchmarks DBP15K, DWY100K, SRPRS and DBP v1.1 [G12]; and temporal KG benchmarks [G09, G10, G17]. Two catalogues mix KG and non-KG datasets: G24's "KG Dataset" column includes text, table and sentiment datasets, and G13 lists GLUE, SQuAD and other text benchmarks among benchmarks for LLM–KG integration.

Category coverage. The only main-table evidence is KG completion and link prediction [G04]. All other categories have no documented use in this batch, although the background table covers entity alignment (C3), temporal and few-shot completion (C4), KGQA (C6), KG evolution and versioning (C10), domain applications (C11) and KG-grounded LLM evaluation (C15).

Primary evidence is thin. Of 25 files, only one standalone article and six chapters of one volume document KG dataset use; 22 files are surveys without own experiments and one is a withdrawal notice. Batch 7 therefore contributes mainly follow-up leads (Section ) rather than new rows.

Scholarly KGs dominate the volume evidence. Three ICADL chapters build or feed the Open Research Knowledge Graph or scholarly relation triples: relation classification on SemEval-2018 Task 7, SciERC and their combination [A20-1], BAO-semantified bioassays [A20-8], and survey-table import of 2,626 papers [A20-35]. Two introduce new data (the Combined corpus; the survey-table dataset on Zenodo), but evaluation is small or absent: one assay [A20-8], no audit of ingested triples [A20-35].

Entity linking for historical text depends on Wikidata and Wikipedia coverage. CLEF HIPE 2020 and NewsEye use Wikidata IDs as gold links; the authors trained the English model on contemporary AIDA because no historical English training data exist, and name missing historical entities in the KBs as a limit [A20-19].

Construction and application papers rarely evaluate the KG itself. The diabetes evidence KG reports four risk-score test cases and no validation [H01]; the lecture-segmentation KG is used only for concept similarity, ignoring relation names [A20-5]; the linked-data crawler reports stop-signal counts, not completeness [A20-31].

Survey-compiled statistics disagree and must be traced to sources. H05 and H20 print a DBpedia row with 400 facts and entity counts that differ by ten (5,044,223 vs 5,044,233); FB15k-237 has 15,028 entities in H25 Table 5 but 14,541 in H15 Table 8 and H20 Table 5; H20 Table 5 appears to swap relation and triple counts for several rows. The most useful inventories for follow-up are H07 Table 2 (semantic table interpretation gold standards with target KGs), H15 Tables 6–8 (split sizes and source links), H16 Table III (multi-modal KGs) and H03 Table 4 (KG-based recommendation datasets).

Category coverage. Main-table evidence falls in KG construction and information extraction, KG retrieval and search, and KG-supported applications only. Placing entity linking to Wikidata [A20-19] under construction and focused linked-data crawling [A20-31] under retrieval and search are reviewer decisions.

The batch is dominated by KG construction from text. 27 of the 45 main rows fall under KG construction and information extraction. The shared benchmarks are WebNLG [J05, J07], TEKGEN [J05, J07], the REBEL dataset [J05, J16] and NYT with Freebase distant labels [J01, J07, J16, J17]; Wikipedia and Wikidata are each used by six papers, mostly as the text and KG sides of distantly supervised alignments.

Distant supervision makes reference sets incomplete. Zhang and Soh report that EDC is penalised on REBEL and Wiki-NRE because their reference triplets are non-exhaustive, extracting about one more triplet per sentence than the reference, while WebNLG (text written from the triplets) does not show this gap [J05, Table 7, PDF p. 15]. Huguet Cabot and Navigli describe their own REBEL dataset as silver data that may keep noise or miss entailed relations [J16, p. 2374]. Precision on these benchmarks therefore partly measures agreement with an incomplete reference.

LLM-era evaluations use very small samples or none. Zhu et al. test on 20–25 instances per dataset and ten sentences for VINE [J09]; KGValidator uses 150 examples per dataset because of API cost [J06]; EDC samples 1,000 test pairs from REBEL and Wiki-NRE [J05]. Theme-specific KGs are scored against author-annotated gold KGs from 20 documents per theme [J02], and the sustainability and Bangla KGs are judged qualitatively only [J04, J03].

New or derived datasets are frequent, but release is uneven. The batch introduces EVB and HAI [J02], VINE [J09], the Math-KG KER/ERC sets [J11], ontology-enriched UMLS-O, FB15K-237O and WN18RR-O [J15], the REBEL dataset [J16], WikiGraphs [J26], and author-built food and sustainability KGs [J01, J04]. Release URLs are printed for J11, J15, J16 and J26 and announced for J09; J02 calls its sets benchmarks without a URL, and J17 gives its location as "blindreview".

Quality assessment evidence comes from two directions. KGValidator re-uses KG completion benchmarks as validation targets and finds the ontology-specific triples of UMLS and WN18RR hard to verify even with retrieved context [J06]. The GeoKG review applies a 20-metric framework to mmkb (DB15K, FB15K, YAGO15K) and UUKG (CHI, NYC) and notes that missing metadata forces default scores for method performance and confidence [J18].

Category coverage and surveys. This batch adds KG-to-text evidence (WikiGraphs, C7) and graph–text retrieval (C8) [J26] but has no direct evidence for entity resolution, KG reasoning, KG maintenance, or the four categories added in Batch 1. Twelve of the 26 files are surveys without own experiments; several compile benchmark statistics that are useful for the survey's dataset section: temporal KG completion [J21, Table 1], temporal KGQA [J22, App. A], temporal KG reasoning [J23], structure-based reasoning [J19, Tables 11–12] and multi-modal KGs [J13, Table II]. Placing LLM evaluation on KG tasks [J09] under task categories rather than KG-grounded evaluation of LLMs is a reviewer decision.

Construction papers introduce KGs but rarely release or evaluate them as KGs. Most C1 rows are dataset introductions of new domain KGs built from proprietary or institutional sources: failure logs [L01], e-commerce text [L02], Sinopec data [L10], earthquake statistics [L17], island data [L19], Sogou web data [L20], Bosch welding data [I22-44, I22-45]. Evaluation usually targets an extraction component, not the KG: AliMe KG instance triples were only spot-checked [L02]; Petro-KG, the Sogou KG and the TCM KG report no quality measure [L10, L20, L29]. Of the 27 standalone papers with rows, only six print a URL for their own data or code [L08, L09, L18, L24, L33, L34]; four offer data on request [L19, L23, L26, L28].

LLM-based construction is evaluated on small, sampled or generated test data. CodeKGC evaluates ADE on 300 random test samples because of API limits [L08]; LLHKG reports only BERTScore on HyperRED [L11]; LLM-ACNC splits 80:20 after GPT-4 augmentation of 2,284 original items to 7,923 [L23]; LLM-TIKG trains on GPT-annotated data, where 1,600 corrected samples gave higher NER precision than 15,000 uncorrected ones (87.88% vs 68.72%) [L24]; the contract-review evaluation has 18 test clauses [L06]; GKG-LLM samples several of its 29 datasets for balance [L18].

Benchmark audits and new benchmarks come mainly from the ISWC 2022 chapters. HybridFC cleans FactBench and uses BirthPlace/DeathPlace because FactBench lets relation-agnostic checkers succeed [I22-27]; Radar Station corrects annotation errors in T2D and Limaye [I22-29]; GNNQ builds nine inductive benchmarks because existing query-embedding benchmarks are transductive [I22-28]; Bio-ML replaces OAEI biomedical tasks with ML-friendly splits [I22-33]; growth snapshots of DBP15K simulate evolving KGs [I22-12]; WDBench uses real Wikidata query logs [I22-41]; DTBM is proposed because BSBM and LUBM do not reflect digital-twin workloads [I22-46]. OneSRPL transfers from WN18RR to WN18 without discussing WN18's inverse-relation leakage (reviewer flag) [L26].

DBpedia and Wikidata are the dominant backbones, mostly as link targets or sources. DBpedia appears in 17 papers and Wikidata in 12, typically for entity linking, enrichment or schema mapping [E20-8, E20-29, E20-40, I22-3, I22-18] rather than as evaluation subjects; exceptions analyse the KGs themselves [E20-31, I22-21] or build benchmarks from them [I22-32, I22-34, I22-41]. Source continuity is a recurring risk: MAG was decommissioned and CS-KG moves to OpenAlex [I22-39]; the Sogou paper notes Freebase's shutdown [L20].

Reported numbers need checking against tables. The ontology-development paper claims better Inheritance Richness although its value is lower than all three baselines and ODCM [L22]; the surveying KG states two incompatible test fractions [L09]; the vulnerability KG reuses hyperparameters identical to the construction-safety paper [L16 vs L14]; REBench lists seven member datasets while calling RELD-RDF six datasets [I22-37].

Category coverage. C1 dominates (57 rows). The volumes add evidence for KG storage and query processing [E20-30, I22-4, I22-24, I22-40, I22-41, I22-46], quality assessment [E20-31, I22-6, I22-20, I22-21, I22-27] and KG-to-text generation [L18, I22-32]. There is no evidence for fairness and bias, KG-grounded LLM evaluation, or KG maintenance and evolution as a separate task; continual entity alignment [I22-12] is placed under entity resolution and ontology archiving [I22-6] under quality assessment, both reviewer decisions. GKG-LLM's commonsense sub-tasks (summarisation, NLI, text classification) are recorded as peripheral because the datasets contain no graph structure [L18].

This batch is dominated by KG completion on a small benchmark core. 44 of the 69 main rows are KG completion and link prediction. FB15k-237 is used by 18 of the 29 primary papers and WN18RR by 14; FB15k (10 papers), NELL-995, WN18 (6 each), UMLS, YAGO3-10 and Freebase (5 each) follow.

Known flaws of FB15k and WN18 are stated but the sets are still used. StAR states that over 80% of WN18 and FB15k test triples can be found in training with another relation and that the sets should no longer be used [M28]; RotatE cites the 81% figure for FB15k [M26]; LiteralE calls the FB15k test set biased [M13]; ConMask notes reversed or synonym triples [M22]. FB15k or WN18 still appear as evaluation sets in M14, M15, M18, M22, M24, M25, M26 and M27.

New datasets are mostly re-cuts of existing KGs. Authors derive FB15k-237-OWE [M04], sparse-entity splits [M14], continual-learning session splits [M08], literal-extended FB15k and FB15k-237 [M13], YAGO39K and M-YAGO39K [M10], DBPedia50k and DBPedia500k [M22], FB40K [M18] and large-scale query sets on FB400k, ogbl-wikikg2 and Freebase [M27]. Only three new KG resources are built from new source documents or databases (besides the dataset-specific co-occurrence graphs of M09): ProcKG from manufacturing documents [M03], BioKG and its five benchmarks from curated biological databases [M06], and DDB14 from the Disease Database [M24]. BioKG is the only one with an explicit limitations section on the data (sparsity, predicted annotations, leakage risk) [M06].

Open-world and inductive evaluation is fragmented. Open-world entity prediction uses FB20k, DBPedia50k and FB15k-237-OWE [M04, M22]; inductive link prediction uses the GraIL splits [M25, M30], random node removal on WN18RR [M24], or splits that the paper does not describe [M19]. ULTRA evaluates on 57 graphs and shows that the Hits@10-with-50-negatives metric published for 8 datasets overestimates performance [M30].

LLM-based evaluation relies on small samples and on Freebase-built QA sets. KG-LLM evaluates ChatGPT and GPT-4 on 100-example subsets because of access limits [M11]; Think-on-Graph samples 1,000 questions from GrailQA and SimpleQuestions and finds Freebase helps more than Wikidata on CWQ and WebQSP because both were built on Freebase [M29]; GIVE runs its prompting and encoder studies on 50 examples per dataset [M12].

Comparisons often reuse published baseline numbers. Baseline results are copied from the original or another paper in M11, M20, M25 and M26 (and runtime figures in M27), so dataset versions and preprocessing are assumed identical rather than checked.

Category coverage. Beyond KG completion, the batch adds multi-hop logical query answering [M05, M27], open KG reasoning with text [M07], rule learning [M14, M21], typing and taxonomy [M10, M16], entity alignment [M16], continual KG embedding [M08], KGQA with LLMs [M12, M29] and two application rows (robotics [M08], social-relationship recognition [M09]). There is no evidence for KG-to-text generation, KG retrieval and search, fairness, storage and query processing, or visualisation.

Two benchmarks carry most of the batch. FB15k-237 is used by 18 of the 30 contributing papers and WN18RR by 16, mainly for link prediction. The leakage-prone originals persist: FB15k appears in six papers and WN18 in four [N07, N13, N14, N17, N20, N23]. Several papers state the leakage or inverse-relation problem and evaluate on the originals anyway [N07, N13, N20]; N14 attributes a baseline's FB15k advantage to the leakage; N23 uses FB15k without discussing it; N22 avoids FB15k for this reason.

Reported dataset statistics are often wrong or inconsistent. Entity, relation or split counts differ from the commonly reported figures or from the paper's own text in N03 (WN18RR entities), N14 (NELL995 entities), N20 (FB15k entities), N23 (YAGO3-10 relations, UMLS training size), N26 and N30 (WN18RR split sizes); FB15K-237N has 14,541 entities in N16 and 13,104 in N12; N24's split figures do not add up. Statistics for the survey should be taken from the original dataset papers, not from user papers.

Triple-classification negatives are rarely documented. N01 and N07 state that FB15k-237 and WN18RR "provide" negative triples without identifying them; N23 builds its own FB15k negatives; N12 does not state the source; N09 corrupts true triples. Classification results on the same dataset name are therefore not comparable across papers.

Inductive, few-shot and sparse settings rely on derived splits. GraIL splits [N08, N18], BERTRL splits ranked against 50 candidates [N15], InGram splits and ILPC [N08], NELL-One [N16] and the DacKGR sparse KGs [N28] are all re-derivations of a few source KGs. N15 reports that 61 of 205 FB15k-237 inductive test triples have no reasoning path; N18 drops NELL-995 because most of its triples are argued to be meaningless or trivial.

LLM-based KGQA converges on Freebase benchmarks. WebQSP and CWQ over Freebase are used by N25, N27 and N29; N25 does not name the KG. MetaQA 2-hop is saturated (many methods above 99%) and EtD reaches 100% on WorldCup2014 [N29]. Out-of-KG transfer of a KG foundation model is tested only on CommonsenseQA [N08].

Domain KGs appear mostly as private or thinly described resources. The steel surface defect KG [N21] and the truck CAN data [N19] come from company-internal sources with no release statement; the biological case studies use DrugBank_FDA, the Decagon polypharmacy data and OhmNet tissue data [N10]; FinDKG [N05], French Royalty with author-written SHACL constraints [N11], DS-KG [N19] and the OpenKG medical QA set [N25] are each used by one paper, the last with no size or schema reported.

Category coverage. The batch is dominated by KG completion (49 rows) and KG reasoning (17 rows). It contains no evidence for ontology and typing, entity resolution, KG-to-text, retrieval, quality refinement, or the four categories added in Batch 1. Temporal completion on ICEWS14 [N16] is the only maintenance-and-evolution row, a reviewer placement; LLM triple extraction for a dialogue system [N06] is placed under construction although the authors call it KG completion.

KG completion still runs on a handful of benchmarks. 46 of the 95 main rows fall under KG completion and link prediction, and 24 papers use FB15k-237 and 21 use WN18RR. FB15k and WN18 remain in 11 papers each, including recent ones [O14, O21, O31]; O14, O27 and O31 state their inverse-relation test leakage, while KG-BERT uses FB15K without comment [O20] and ComplEx mentions WN18's inverse relations only when analysing its embeddings [O24].

Benchmark audits report concrete defects. Rossi et al. find that 212 WN18RR test entities never appear in training (about 6.7% of test facts unpredictable) and that converting Freebase CVT nodes into cliques made FB15k artificially dense and semantically altered [O27]. LiterallyWikidata reports that YAGO3-10 contains duplicate relations (isAffiliatedTo, playsFor) that make prediction easy and that NELL-995 triples are nonsensical or overly generic [I21-30]. InductivE reports that the CN-100K split uses only 2.4% of triples for validation and test, chosen by confidence [O17]; HoGRN argues that common KGC datasets are denser than real KGs and evaluates on sparse subsets [O11].

Freebase's retirement forces workarounds. KICGPTv2 maps FB15k-237 entities to Wikidata QIDs to obtain context [O22]; ESTHER infers a class hierarchy for FB15k-237 because Freebase has none [I21-16]; Rossi et al. recover CVTs from the last Freebase dump [O27].

Text- and LLM-based completion depends on text attached to benchmarks, which differs per dataset. KG-BERT uses synset definitions for WN18RR, descriptions for FB15k-237 and names only for UMLS [O20]; PEMLM states it needs good entity and relation descriptions [O19]; HSAE adds descriptions to ICEWS14 [O13]; KICGPTv2 reports that unnatural relation labels in FB15k-237 and WN18RR hurt LLM relation prediction [O22].

Wikidata is both a source of new benchmarks and a subject of study. New Wikidata-derived datasets include WD20K for inductive hyper-relational link prediction [I21-5], LiterallyWikidata [I21-30], Wiki27K [O15] and the 250 WT table set [I21-18]; editor edit histories are released as benchmarks for retention and recommendation [I21-3, I21-10].

Resource and in-use chapters report scale more often than evaluation. AgroLD (over 900M triples), CKGG (1.50B triples), the EU Knowledge Graph (96M triples), the ERA KG (13.8M triples) and MMM describe construction and access [I21-29, I21-25, I21-37, I21-38, I21-36]; only CKGG reports a sampled quality evaluation (79% coverage of 295 study-guide locations; manual checks of consolidated entities) [I21-25], while AgroLD reports count- and SPARQL-based checks [I21-29]. Several deployments rely on private data that are not released [I21-26, I21-27, I21-34, I21-41].

Benchmark versions are reported inconsistently. I21-8 states that LC-QuAD 1.0 uses DBpedia 2016-04 and QALD-9 DBpedia 2016-10; I21-19 states the reverse. Version statements should be taken from the benchmark papers, not from user papers.

Category coverage. This batch adds evidence for ontology translation and development [I21-15, I21-26, I21-32, I21-34, I21-35], query processing over ontologies [I21-12, I21-22, I21-27], fact checking and markup or annotation quality [I21-16, I21-20, I21-31], and collaborative KG maintenance [I21-3, I21-10]. It contains no direct evidence for KG-to-text generation, fairness and bias, KG visualisation, or KG-grounded evaluation of LLMs.

The completion and reasoning line rests on a small set of benchmarks. FB15k-237 is used by 17 of the 25 papers with rows, WN18RR by 13 and NELL-995 by 9; YAGO3-10 and UMLS follow with four each. Most rows on these benchmarks are consolidated because several benchmarks serve an identical training-and-testing role, and many papers copy baseline numbers from earlier work rather than re-running them [P08, P12, P19, P23, P24, P25, P30].

Leakage-prone benchmarks are still reported. MRGAT, McRL and QuatE report FB15k and WN18 next to their filtered successors [P18, P19, P30]; HAKE states that FB15k suffers from test leakage and still uses it to match TKRL's setting [P12]. FGEM, KG2E and ProjE use FB15k or WN18 without discussing leakage [P07, P13, P29].

Inductive evaluation has its own benchmark family. The GraIL v1–v4 splits of WN18RR, FB15k-237 and NELL-995 are used by RED-GNN, KRLM and GLAR [P04, P08, P24]; NSAP reports v1–v4 splits without naming their source and omits YAGO3-10 because no widely adopted inductive split exists [P23]. KRLM adds 13 InGram splits with unseen relations [P08], Memory-KGC uses Wikidata5M-Ind [P15], and KoPA builds its own inductive CoDeX-S re-splits [P14]. GLAR does not compare text-based methods because the GraIL splits lack descriptions [P24].

Path-reasoning papers evaluate on per-relation task subsets. VRNet, MemoryPath, MARLPaR and the CNN-BiLSTM model report MAP or Hits on selected NELL-995 or FB15k-237 query relations [P05, P16, P26, P27]; MARLPaR covers 9 NELL-995 tasks [P26]. HMLS rebuilds few-shot versions of FB15K-237, NELL-995 and Wikidata with dataset-specific frequency thresholds [P21]. Scores are therefore tied to task selection and are hard to compare with whole-graph link prediction.

LLM-based methods keep the standard benchmarks. KRLM (Llama2-7b), KoPA (Alpaca-7B) and PPENet (Qwen2.5-7B) are evaluated on the same KGC benchmarks as embedding models [P08, P14, P28]; KoPA restricts evaluation to triple classification with hard negatives [P14]. KnowledgeNavigator answers WebQSP over a full 3.12B-triple Freebase dump and MetaQA 2- and 3-hop sets [P10]. The KG-infused fine-tuning paper names T-REx as its KG but not its evaluation benchmark or backbone [P09].

New or domain KGs come with restricted access. PPENet introduces the Emergency Fire KG from a non-public incident workbook and releases only a privacy-filtered subset [P28]; KompaRe uses YAGO and a Covid-19 graph with author-built query sets [P11]; NSAP states data are available on request [P23]. ProjE reuses DBpedia and SemMedDB fact-checking question sets from earlier work [P29].

Category coverage. Evidence concentrates in KG completion (C4) and KG reasoning (C5). KGQA has one paper [P10], quality assessment one (fact checking) [P29], construction one (EFKG) [P28] and KG-supported applications one [P09]. There is no direct evidence for ontology and typing, entity resolution, KG-to-text, retrieval, maintenance or the four added categories.

A completion-only batch built on two benchmarks. FB15k-237 is used by 16 papers and WN18RR by 15, nearly always as the default transductive pair. Six papers still evaluate on FB15k and WN18 as main benchmarks [Q06, Q08, Q10, Q19, Q27, Q28]; two of them discuss redundancy or inverse relations [Q06, Q08], while two other papers drop FB15k and WN18 explicitly because of test leakage [Q11, Q16]. Meilicke et al. add a critique of the replacement: FB15k-237 contains no test case solvable by a one-atom C rule even though training supports such rules, which they call "a bit unrealistic" [Q06].

Inductive KGC rests on one family of splits, evaluated under different protocols. The GraIL v1-v4 subsets of WN18RR, FB15k-237 and NELL-995 are used by five papers [Q01, Q09, Q15, Q22, Q30] and NELL-995 v1 by a sixth [Q26]. New derived benchmarks re-combine or filter these splits: fully inductive NELL-995 and FB15k-237 sets [Q09, reused by Q30], empty-subgraph sets [Q30] and InGram's FB-*/NL-* sets [Q26]. Ranking is done against 49 sampled negatives [Q09], 50 candidates [Q22] or all entities, and one paper warns that its `ind-test' choice may differ from others [Q26], so scores are not directly comparable across papers.

Reported statistics and results contain checkable inconsistencies. WN18RR is listed with 18 relations and 141,422 triplets [Q03]; FB15K-237 and WNRR with 14,505 and 40,559 entities [Q31]; a FB15K-237 few-shot split with 231 relations [Q29]; Hits@1 above MRR for one model [Q30]; two different MRR values for the same model [Q02]; and NELL-995 gains claimed without a results table [Q15]. None of these papers explains the differences, which supports recording dataset versions explicitly in the survey.

LLM-based KGC narrows evaluation by design. Context limits force a base model to pre-select candidates [Q02, Q12]; both papers evaluate only transductively [Q02, Q12]. KGR3 maps FB15k-237 entities to Wikidata because Freebase is deprecated [Q12]. SuKE evaluates triple classification with author-generated negatives and a KGQA transfer test whose 500 questions were generated and judged by LLMs [Q25].

New datasets are introduced mostly as derived splits or private domain KGs. Wiki79k, Wiki143k and CFamily support the new triple set prediction task under a partial open-world and a closed-world assumption [Q24]; IM-1M links MovieLens 1M to IMDB attributes [Q05]; PGPR turns four Amazon review categories into KGs [Q07]; the spacecraft fault KG is described only by its entity and relation category counts [Q23]. Five papers state that data are available only on request [Q02, Q20, Q25, Q29, Q30].

Category coverage. C4 holds most rows. KG reasoning (C5) is represented by RL path reasoning and rule learning [Q03, Q13, Q14]; KG-supported applications (C11) by two recommendation papers [Q05, Q07]; ontology use (C2) by the NELL-995 schema graph that initialises unseen relations [Q09], also used by Q30; KGQA (C6) only by the LLM-generated CoDeX-S question set [Q25]. There is no evidence for construction, entity resolution, KG-to-text, retrieval, quality, maintenance or the four added categories.

LLM-for-ontology-engineering evaluations rest on a few small CQ benchmarks. Three chapters evaluate LLM-generated competency questions or ontologies against author CQs: four ontologies from CORAL and the Wi\'sniewski et al. dataset [E24-1], five ontologies normalised into the new LLM4KE dataset [E24-7], and the 14 African Wildlife CQs [E24-38]. Validity is decided by SBERT similarity with fixed or empirical thresholds [E24-1, E24-7] or by one expert [E24-38]; the single-domain Wine ontology serves as gold standard for NeOn-GPT [E24-4]. These datasets count CQs in tens, not thousands.

Ontology matching reuses OAEI tracks, and a new ML split targets an evaluation flaw. LLMs4OM evaluates on 20 tasks from six OAEI tracks [E24-3]; Hertling et al. release stratified 20/10/70 train/validation/test splits for Anatomy, BioDiv, Knowledge Graph and Bio-ML because systems were sampling training data from reference alignments, which the authors state is against OAEI rules (p. 239) [E24-34]. Bio-ML remains hard for LLMs, including a domain-specific model [E24-3].

Wikidata and DBpedia are the most reused KGs, mostly as sources rather than benchmarks. Each appears in five chapters. Benchmark-like uses are the Wikidata class-membership set [E24-2], LC-QuAD-based SPARQL generation [E24-5], DBpedia Person subgraphs for relation extraction [E24-8] and four DBpedia snapshots for embedding updates [E24-30]; the other uses are demo endpoints, label sources or quality-assessment targets [E24-6, E24-21, E24-40, E24-41, E24-42, E24-48]. Two chapters name possible pre-training exposure of the models to these KGs as an unaddressed limitation [E24-2, E24-8].

Many KGs are introduced without evaluation, and access ranges from open dumps to none. Industry chapters describe internal KGs with no release [E24-11, E24-12, E24-15, E24-16, E24-17]. Open cultural-heritage and research-information KGs are served through endpoints and portals: ArtSampo on a restricted read-only endpoint [E24-18], NFDI4Culture-KG [E24-22], the Helmholtz KG with CC BY 4.0 data and Zenodo dumps [E24-23], MusicBO with copyright-restricted source texts [E24-29], FinEstLawSampo [E24-35], CLARA on Zenodo [E24-36], CoinSampo [E24-45] and GTKG behind a free API key [E24-49]. For a dataset survey, these are resource descriptions, not tested benchmarks.

Quality assessment evidence shifts from rule-based to LLM-assisted checks. LLM classifiers flag missing and incorrect instanceOf relations in Wikidata and CaLiGraph, with 40.9% of analysed errors traced to the KGs [E24-2]; GPT-4 turns compliance rules and CQs into SPARQL validation queries for OPC UA Robotics and SAREF [E24-9]. SHACL shapes are extracted from schemas and mappings [E24-26] or mined evolutionarily from data [E24-28]. KGHeartBeat finds that SPARQL endpoint availability dominates the quality scores of DBpedia language editions (8/100 to 57/100) [E24-41].

Synthetic or narrow data limit several conclusions. LLM-KG-Bench uses small synthetic Turtle graphs [E24-5]; SolidBench data are so uniform that Bloom filters prune no links [E24-32]; root-cause analysis uses simulated observations [E24-50]; critical-path identification is judged by experts on three supplier subgraphs (company names anonymised) with no gold labels [E24-31].

Category coverage and placement decisions. The batch has no evidence for KG completion and link prediction, KG-to-text generation or fairness, and only one QA chapter [E24-44]. Reviewer placements: semantic table annotation under ontology, schema and typing [E24-6]; ontology matching and DCAT schema alignment under entity resolution and KG integration [E24-3, E24-27, E24-34]; EL++ subsumption embeddings and supply-chain path identification under KG reasoning [E24-31, E24-39]; RDF2vec updating under KG maintenance and evolution [E24-30]; KG resource introductions with portals under KG construction [E24-18, E24-35, E24-45].

Freebase-era QA benchmarks still dominate KGQA evaluation. WebQSP is used in 12 papers and CWQ in 7, almost always over Freebase or a Freebase subset [T01, T03, T04, T06, T09, T13, T15, T19, T20, T24, T26, T28]. Only one paper states that Freebase is outdated and re-maps WebQSP to Wikidata, which keeps 1,466 of the 1,639 test questions [T24]. MetaQA, the second benchmark line, is described as saturated [T04] and as simple, narrow-domain and partly answerable with fewer hops than labelled [T22]; its originating paper itself lists the single-hop, noise-free and template-limited nature of WikiMovies as the reason for building it [T30].

KG incompleteness is simulated in many incompatible ways. Random deletion of 50% of triples [T03, T09] or of KB triples [T07], removal of 50% of relations [T15], targeted deletion of crucial gold-path triples at 20–80% [T19], dropping 5–10% of extracted triplets [T23], and four edge-perturbation heuristics at controlled levels [T12]. Scores reported as "incomplete KG" therefore are not comparable across papers.

LLM-era papers evaluate on sampled subsets and address contamination unevenly. Test sets are sampled to 300/600 [T13], 1,000 [T19, T26] or repeated samples of 100 and 500 questions [T22]; ChatGPT is compared on 300 questions [T06]. Contamination is raised as a possibility [T06, T18], measured for synthetic training data (2.57% above cosine 0.85) [T20], or countered by entity shuffling [T23] and by filtering out questions an LLM already answers [T26].

New datasets are increasingly synthetic or LLM-generated. Benchmarks introduced in this batch range from human-curated (ComplexQuestions from search logs [T16]; MetaQA templates, paraphrases and audio [T30]; PeCoQ with linguist paraphrases [T25]) to LLM-generated or LLM-refined (OKGQA queries [T12], Un-Amb regenerated from gold SPARQL [T13], GraphSynth trajectories and GraphWalkerBench [T20], the ReasoningLM adaptation corpus [T28], the PRM question set drafted by Gemini [T08]). MINE articles are LLM-generated, and RAKG adds per-article standard KGs whose construction is not described [T27].

Domain KGs built for applications are small, rarely released and weakly evaluated. The Vietnamese tourism QA set has 300 pairs and inconsistent KG size statements [T10]; the Liao Dynasty KG reports no construction quality figures [T07]; the PRM corpus is not public [T08]; the PrimeKG Text-to-Cypher benchmark has 50 questions [T14]. The e-commerce QA dataset is the exception, released on Hugging Face with code [T02].

Category coverage. KG question answering accounts for 49 of 61 rows. The batch adds construction evidence (C1) from five papers [T02, T07, T08, T10, T27], one domain ontology [T08], KG-guided RAG retrieval [T23] and KG-grounded evaluation of LLMs [T06, T12]. There is no evidence for entity resolution, completion, reasoning as a separate task, KG-to-text, quality, maintenance or the four added categories other than C15. Placement of KG2RAG under KG retrieval [T23] and of EQAS under KG-supported applications [T02] is a reviewer decision.

KGQA dominates and runs on a few Freebase benchmarks. 71 of the main-table rows are KG question answering. WebQSP and Freebase each appear in 13 papers and CWQ in 10, almost always over per-question or merged Freebase subgraphs rather than the full KG [U06, U07, U09, U11–U13, U15, U16, U18, U20, U26, U27, U31]. Subgraph sizes for the same benchmark range from 1.3M entities [U20] to 1.9M entities [U16, U18] and a single 106M-triple graph [U31], so reported scores are not strictly comparable.

Benchmark split and count reporting is inconsistent. WebQSP is given as 4,737 [U07, U13], 4,037 [U18] or 4,837 questions with splits summing to 4,737 [U12]; BiNet reports 2,950/1,560 [U16] and RAPL 2,826/1,628 [U26]. Several papers copy baselines from earlier work [U07, U13, U20], which makes such discrepancies hard to detect.

Incomplete-KG settings are synthetic. Robustness to missing facts is tested by deleting 50% or 70% of edges at random [U11, U13, U16, U27]; BiNet notes that on the complete KG simple traversal reaches 99–100% coverage [U16]. Only WebQSP-Wiki introduces incompleteness from a real KG mismatch [U12].

Contamination and popularity bias motivate new test sets. FiDeLiS argues WebQSP and CWQ feature popular entities likely seen in LLM pre-training and adds CR-LT-KGQA (200 questions) and a 300-question MedQA subset [U09]; KEQA builds an unseen-predicate split SimpleQ_Missing [U24]; CONVEX releases ConvQuestions because existing benchmarks are one-shot or template-generated [U28].

Domain KGs are built by the authors and rarely released. Diabetes (DiaKG-based) [U01], malware literature [U02], industrial [U04], Form 10-K chunk graph [U05], Greek legal and encyclopedic corpora [U21], graduate admissions [U25] and chemistry ontologies [U29] are evaluated on author-made question sets, scored with an LLM judge, BERTScore or RAGAS [U04, U05, U25], compared only with the same LLM without retrieval [U02], or with no baseline at all [U05]. U14 does not name its KG at all.

Commonsense QA pairs benchmarks with ConceptNet and records its gaps. CommonsenseQA and OpenBookQA are answered over ConceptNet subgraphs [U17, U20, U30]; JointLK attributes 39 of 100 errors to missing ConceptNet evidence and MRGNN notes ConceptNet lacks negative relations [U17, U30].

Category coverage. This batch adds evidence for KG-grounded testing of QA models with YAGO4 [U23], KG-based fact verification on FACTKG [U19] and conversational recommendation over DBpedia [U08]. Link prediction appears only as a component study on WN18RR/FB15k-237 [U03, U11] or on QA-specific KGs [U16, U29]. LEGO is placed under KG reasoning (query-tree execution) rather than KGQA; this is a reviewer decision.

Freebase-based KGQA benchmarks still carry most of the evaluation. Thirteen papers answer questions over Freebase or a Freebase subset [V12, V14, V15, V17, V19, V21, V23, V25, V26, V27, V28, V30, V31]; ten use WebQSP and seven CWQ. Authors also state their limits: PYTHIA calls WebQSP and CWQ best-case scenarios for fine-tuned systems with virtually no zero-shot questions [V17]; KGT5 notes MetaQA is template-based with little linguistic variation and that full Freebase, with CVT nodes, does not suit text-based models [V28]; Singh et al. could use only 3,253 of 5,000 LC-QuAD questions because the benchmark was built on an older DBpedia release [V13].

KG incompleteness is simulated by random triple removal. V14 keeps a fraction of the KB, V23 removes 10%, 30% or 50% of triples, and V27 and V28 use a 50% KG setting; V27 excludes PathQuestion from that setting because its KGs are so small that removal could disconnect subgraphs. Reported robustness therefore depends on the sampling procedure rather than on observed missing facts.

Multimodal KG datasets are built by attaching web images to existing KGs. FB-IMG [V01], MMKG [V11], FB15k-237-IMG and WN18-IMG [V05], CoDEx-Mul [V09] and CoDEx-IMG-R [V06] all extend FB15K, WordNet or CoDEx. Authors acknowledge noisy crawled images [V01], filter them with annotators [V09] or release only image links [V11]. V05 calls its WordNet dataset both WN18-IMG and WN18RR-IMG.

Several new benchmarks are thinly documented or not released. Evolving-QA [V02] and CoSuQue [V23] are described only by size and question types; AG-LLM-mm will be released upon acceptance [V10]; CoSuQue and SCR's data are available only on request [V23, V27]. By contrast, MMKG has a repository, a Zenodo record and a BSD-3-Clause licence [V11], and CoDEx-Mul is shared through a public folder [V09].

Graphs built on the fly from text are evaluated with LLM-generated tasks and LLM judges. Graph2Eval generates agent tasks from KGs over 16 papers and 8 websites and scores web tasks with an LLM evaluator [V08]; GraphRAG-Bench generates and refines questions with GPT-4.1 and reports that common RAG corpora yield sparse, fragmented graphs [V32]; StepChain GraphRAG [V29] and Cognitive Weave [V02] construct graphs during inference.

Category coverage. Evidence concentrates in KGQA (36 rows) and KG completion (12 rows, including temporal [V04], multimodal [V01, V05, V06, V09] and large-scale seq2seq completion [V28]). Entity resolution has one paper [V11]; KG construction has five rows (continual multimodal [V03], cyber-threat attack graphs [V10], MMKG [V11], an automobile KG [V24]). WebNLG KG-to-text data appear only as instruction-tuning data inside a KGQA pipeline [V25], so this batch has no direct KG-to-text evidence. Event forecasting on ICEWS [V07] is placed under KG-supported applications and GraphRAG evaluation [V29, V32] under KG retrieval and search; both placements are reviewer decisions.

Temporal KG completion rests on a few ICEWS and GDELT subsets, under incompatible protocols. ICEWS14 and ICEWS05-15 each appear in ten papers and GDELT in seven [W01, W04, W05, W08, W10, W11, W16, W17, W18, W27]. The same names hide different settings: W10 re-splits ICEWS and GDELT for interpolation, W01 uses buffered chronological splits with temporal gaps, W16 reports raw metrics with ground-truth history, and W08 applies time-aware filtering and assigns infinite rank when the answer is missing from the sampled subgraph. Scores on `ICEWS14' are therefore not comparable across these papers without the protocol.

Authors themselves question the temporal benchmarks. Messner et al. describe both ICEWS datasets as small and very sparse, dominated by one-time relations and entity-driven predictions, and report that most TKGC models fail to beat the rule-based TED on GDELT [W27]. ChronoR notes that the ICEWS subsets keep only the most frequent entities and suggests the need for more sophisticated datasets [W05]; HSAE reports smaller gains on small datasets [W10].

Multimodal KG completion reuses the FB15K/DB15K/YAGO15K line with varying modality sources and test protocols. HRGAT takes images and numerical literals from MMKG and texts from KG-BERT [W12]; HFR-MKGC uses DB15K, MKG-W and MKG-Y [W09]; LAFA uses FB15k-237-IMG and WN18-IMG [W15]; AMC gives the image source only as public resources [W02]; ViSR-KGC filters test sets to unique-answer queries [W31]. VISTA avoids WN18 because of test leakage and introduces VTKG-I and VTKG-C with triplet-level images, aligned manually through WordNet synsets [W32].

New KGQA benchmarks are mostly generated and LLM-paraphrased. STQAD (10,000 spatio-temporal questions paraphrased with ChatGPT) [W22], TimelineKGQA sets over ICEWS and the CronQuestions KG [W28] and VISPATH-Bench (2,000 LLM-generated multi-hop visual questions over Wikidata5M) [W30] are all synthetic. TwiRGCN moves from CronQuestions to the manually curated TimeQuestions because of reported spurious correlations [W29], while TempoQR still uses CronQuestions and adds a time-corrupted TKG setting [W26]. MIRA-KG builds its own MMKG for ScienceQA, which is not a native KGQA benchmark [W20].

Application and construction papers rely on unreleased, author-built KGs with small evaluations. The Dutch civil registry KG cannot be shared and was evaluated by 13 experts [W03]; the public-opinion MMKG uses one baseline and an unreleased 300-event set [W06]; DSRAG's documentation KG is unnamed and scored by an LLM evaluator on 100 questions [W07]; the deep foundation pit MMKG is confidential and validated on a single project [W13]; SKG-VLA's 1.4 million scene graphs come from an internal pipeline with no release stated [W25]. Richpedia is the exception: a released multimodal KG with a permanent URL and repository [W23].

Benchmark critique also appears for agent memory. Zep's authors judge the Deep Memory Retrieval benchmark inadequate (about 60 messages per conversation, single-turn fact questions, ambiguous phrasing) and add LongMemEval [W33].

Category coverage. This batch gives no direct evidence for ontology and typing, entity resolution, KG-to-text generation, quality assessment, maintenance and evolution, fairness, or KG-grounded LLM evaluation. KG storage and query processing is represented only by the MeGraS demonstration [W19] and KG exploration by graph-pattern discovery [W03]. The dynamic-KG review [W14] is excluded.

The same TKG benchmark name covers different versions, and papers mix their statistics. ICEWS14 is reported with 7,128 entities and 72,826 / 8,941 / 8,963 quadruples [X19, X31] and with 6,869 entities and 74,845 / 8,514 / 7,371 [X05, X16; ICEWS14* in X31]. X25 reports 6,869 entities with the 72,826 / 8,941 / 8,963 split, and X22 reports 7,128 entities with the 74,845 / 8,514 / 7,371 split. ICEWS05-15 appears with 10,094 entities and 368,868 training quadruples [X05, X16], with 10,488 and 386,962 [X19, X31], with 10,094 and 368,962 [X25] and with 10,488 and 368,868 [X22]. GDELT appears as a 500-entity subset with 341,961 validation and test quadruples [X19, X31], the same subset with 34,196 [X25], and a 7,691-entity version [X22]. A survey that pools results by benchmark name would mix interpolation and extrapolation splits; reporting the split and its statistics is necessary.

Temporal KGQA rests on two benchmarks with inconsistent size reports. CronQuestions (410k questions, 350k / 30k / 30k) is used by four papers [X15, X20, X29, X30] and TimeQuestions by three [X15, X29, X30]. TimeQuestions is described as 16,000 questions [X29], as 16,181 questions with a Table 5 total of 16,859 [X30], and as 9,708 / 3,236 / 3,237 [X15]. MultiTQ and the TimelineKGQA datasets appear only in X15, which samples 20% of MultiTQ training data. RTA evaluates on CronQuestions only and its authors plan a new TKGQA dataset because of the limitations of existing ones [X20].

Multimodal KGC benchmarks differ in image coverage and are often under-documented. FB15k-237-IMG and WN18-IMG (ten images per entity) are used by X08 and X23; DB15K, MKG-W and MKG-Y by X21 and X32; multimodal WN9, FB15k-237 and WN18RR by X18, where only 19.1% of WN18RR entities have images. X21 and X09 give no image source or count per entity, X21 gives no dataset statistics, and X12 does not name its evaluation dataset at all. X34 evaluates "multimodal KG reasoning" on FB15K, WN18 and FB15K-237 with injected noise, calls them UCI datasets and does not define the task or metric.

New resources are justified by gaps, but their own evaluation varies widely. ArCo reports ontology tests (18 inference tests, 29 error-provocation tests, 53 CQs), a linking threshold chosen by manual inspection, and stated gaps such as missing English labels [X03]. DBLP-QuAD states that its questions are synthetic, that about 80% of valid/test data share structure with training, and that full titles do not reflect user queries [X04]. AceKG reports no quality evaluation of its 3.13 billion triples [X01]; AISecKG tests NER on 13 sentences [X02]. Derived evaluation sets are often built by the method authors and tested only on their own model: ICEWS05-filter [X16], YAGO11k-ST, Wikidata12k-ST and ICEWS05-ST, whose locations are coordinates of Chinese cities assigned even to US entities [X26], and the Visual Genome MMKG-grounded pretraining set [X11].

Domain and application KGs are rarely released or sized. The steel product-development KG [X13], the traffic-accident KG [X34] and the wildfire KG [X14] report no triple counts; the opera KG OpeMKG reports 35,558 triples [X10]. None of the four is released, and their evaluations are case studies [X13], 10 competency questions [X14], an unattributed test set [X34] or none for the KG itself [X10]. Exceptions that release data are the C-MAPSS TKGs on IEEE DataPort [X27], AISecKG on GitHub [X02] and the FFOnto documentation [X14].

Availability statements are weak in journal papers. Six papers say data are available on request [X05, X18, X19, X24, X30, X35]. X25 says the data used are confidential and X29 says no data was used, although both evaluate only on public benchmarks; X26 has an empty Data availability heading. Code URLs are printed by X09, X16, X17, X20, X22, X31 and X32; resource URLs by X01, X02, X03, X04, X14 and X27.

Category coverage. KG completion (C4) dominates with 24 rows from 19 papers, followed by KG question answering (C6, 13 rows). Construction (C1), ontology (C2) and entity linking (C3) evidence comes from the resource papers [X01, X02, X03, X10, X13, X14]. C8 holds the multimodal RAG papers [X07, X17] and the steel-KG retrieval case [X13]. There is no evidence for KG-to-text generation, quality refinement as a task, maintenance and evolution, or the four categories added in Batch 1. Placing DBLP-QuAD's template-based KGQA dataset under C6 rather than C1, and spatiotemporal multi-hop LLM reasoning [X24] under C5, are reviewer decisions.

Most evidence introduces a new domain KG, and almost nothing is shared. 25 of the 62 main rows are KG construction rows, and most papers build their own resource: CKG (about 20 million nodes) [Y04], GenomicKB (347 million entities) [Y16], KnowLife (542,689 facts) [Y21], LMKG (403,784 entities) [Y22], MatKG (5.4 million triples) [Y23], KG-FM (2.53 million nodes) [Y13], WorldKG (828,550,751 triples) [Y30], GeoOutageKG [Y17], MEKG [Y28], propnet [Y25], FoodKG [Y15], XAI4Wind [Y31] and SciToolKG [Y26]. Only two families recur across papers: Wikidata [Y29, Y30] and UMLS [Y21, Y24]. MatKG cites MEKG and propnet as prior materials KGs (background table), the only explicit cross-link between resources of this batch.

Construction quality is measured by sampled precision, not recall. Precision is estimated from manually judged samples: 22,002 facts by four annotators with Fleiss' Kappa 0.505 [Y21]; 1,000 triplets judged by doctors (94%) [Y22]; 100 LLM extractions (F1 0.9898) [Y13]; 100 triplets per model rated by two experts [Y18]; the 150 highest-confidence extractions (Precision@150 79.33%) [Y02]; 1,000 entity-class pairs (97.9% to 100%) [Y30]. Three papers state that recall or automatic evaluation is impossible without a gold standard [Y02, Y18, Y21]. Several resource papers report no quantitative evaluation of the constructed KG's content [Y01, Y07 (PKG), Y16, Y17, Y28, Y31].

KG-enhanced LLM QA relies on small author-built test sets. Test sets have 150 questions judged by experts [Y13], 60 questions with manual gold answers [Y19], 311 true/false and 306 multiple-choice questions reviewed by experts [Y12], and 1,200 expert-verified TutorQA pairs [Y18]; only MKG-Rank uses existing benchmarks (medical subsets of JMMLU, CMMLU and Global MMLU) [Y24]. Baseline LLMs are usually run without the KG, so gains mainly measure access to the KG.

Template-generated questions over the authors' own KG give near-ceiling scores. BEm-KGQA reaches 98.2% accuracy on questions scripted from 2,080 triples [Y11]; on FoodKG's synthetic set, BAMnet reaches an overall F1 of 95.5 with gold topic entities and question types, and the authors note that there is no lexical gap between questions and KG [Y15].

KG quality is also judged indirectly through downstream gains. LMKG is compared with two other medical KGs by the improvement it gives to NER and RE models [Y22]; Rephetio drug-indication prediction on Wikidata improves with successive Wikidata versions [Y29]; propnet benchmarks property models against experimental refractive indices [Y25]; CKG is shown through reanalyses of six published proteomics studies [Y04].

Category coverage. Besides construction (C1) and applications (C11, 15 rows), the batch adds ontology and taxonomy evidence [Y07, Y27, Y30], temporal KG completion on ICEWS14, ICEWS05-15 and GDELT [Y06], prerequisite link prediction on LectureBankCD [Y18], KG maintenance through crowdsourced curation of the Disease Ontology in Wikidata [Y29], and graph query processing [Y16, Y28]. There is no evidence for entity resolution as a task, KG reasoning, KG-to-text generation, fairness, visualisation or KG-grounded evaluation of LLMs. Placing KGNN's drug-drug interaction prediction under KG-supported applications [Y20] and Wikidata drug-indication prediction under link prediction [Y29] are reviewer decisions.

Most evidence is new resources, not reused benchmarks. Of the 78 families, 71 occur in a single chapter. Resource chapters introduce domain KGs (League of Nations Sampo [E26-1], ArtKB [E26-4], MappingChange [E26-5], EthereumKG [E26-7], SIDEKICK [E26-14], BOLD [E26-17]), ontologies (OntoPFAS [E26-2], DBC [E26-8], SemTS [E26-10], AgentO [E26-16]) and benchmarks (CUBE-MT [E26-6], CR-TKGQA [E26-9], Bench4KE [E26-12], HERTy-Wiki [E26-15]); In-Use chapters add proprietary or project KGs (Thales Alenia Space VKG [E26-21], WISER KG [E26-23], KGIH [E26-24], mdevKG [E26-27]). Established community benchmarks are few: WatDiv and the EYE deep-taxonomy benchmark [E26-3], Text2KGBench [E26-4], TempQA-WD [E26-9], the DBpedia SPARQL Benchmark [E26-13] and the OAEI Conference track [E26-18].

Wikidata is the one recurring backbone, in many roles. Nine chapters use it: as the source KG (ArtKB, CUBE-MT) [E26-4, E26-6], the alignment target for enrichment (E26-1, E26-5), the QA KG with refreshed answers [E26-9], the source of a typing benchmark [E26-15], the grounding for generated training conversations [E26-19], the gold labels for name reconciliation [E26-20] and the CH entity layer of a deployed retrieval system [E26-26]. Several chapters report Wikidata-specific weaknesses: low linkage precision (0.45) due to multiple same-name entities and sparse descriptions [E26-5], descriptions that restate types and leak answers [E26-15], and noisy, sparse entries [E26-19].

LLMs are now a construction tool, checked on small manual samples. LLMs extract articles (GPT-4; 100 single-page and 50 multi-page checks) [E26-5], drug-label facts and ontology mappings (Gemini 2.5 Flash; 980 mappings checked, 96.7% correct) [E26-14], agent-workflow instances (24 of 66 translations reviewed) [E26-16], news triples (105 annotated entity pairs) [E26-25], cleaning rules for industrial databases [E26-21] and CACAO triples (preliminary Text2KGBench scores) [E26-4]. None reports a full-scale accuracy audit of the resulting KG.

In-Use evidence is largely not reusable. The Thales Alenia Space data and tool are confidential [E26-21]; Bosch releases only a simulated mock KG [E26-27]; the WISER API is partner-only [E26-23]; the newsroom corpus is copyrighted and available on request [E26-25]; no release of the generated Wikipedia/Wikidata conversations is stated [E26-19]. Licences also constrain reuse: CC BY-NC-SA for the DBC ontology [E26-8], and a conflict between CC-BY-4.0 and a non-commercial statement for OntoPFAS [E26-2].

Evaluation is frequently self-referential. RAG is scored against the authors' own deployed pipeline [E26-21]; ontology coverage is measured against the authors' own competency questions [E26-8, E26-10]; energy alignments are created by the authors without reported agreement [E26-18]; expert surveys use convenience samples or very small groups (51 partners and five workshop participants [E26-6]; two curators [E26-26]; 14 stakeholders [E26-27]). Internal inconsistencies flagged in Section should be resolved before citing figures.

Category coverage and placement. The batch is concentrated in KG construction (C1), ontology and typing (C2), integration (C3) and applications (C11). It adds one KG-to-text row (KG-grounded conversation generation [E26-19]) and one KG-grounded LLM evaluation row (cultural diversity of generative models [E26-6]); it contains no evidence for KG completion, maintenance and evolution, or fairness. Reviewer placements: ontology matching [E26-18] under C3; KG entity typing [E26-15] under C2; the BOLD agent benchmark [E26-17] and the Kolibrie fraud scenario [E26-3] under C11; faceted scholarly search [E26-22] under C8.

Domain KG construction dominates, and most of these KGs stay with their authors. KG construction and information extraction accounts for 17 of the 43 main rows. Authors build domain KGs for meteorology and agriculture [AA03], aviation risk [AA06], Tang Dynasty artifacts [AA07], power grid dispatching and equipment [AA08, AA14], aquaculture disease [AA09], food safety [AA16], intangible cultural heritage [AA22], construction safety standards [AA23], costume heritage [AA25] and equipment maintenance [AA29]. Their data are available only on request [AA07, AA12, AA23], cannot be shared [AA13], are confidential [AA29], or come with no availability statement [AA03, AA06, AA08, AA09, AA14, AA16].

Many construction papers report no quantitative evaluation of the KG. Validity is argued from a single query or case example [AA06, AA08, AA14, AA16, AA28] or from one document [AA21]; Cn-MAKG reports only node and relation counts and leaves evaluation to future work [AA03]. Where evaluation exists it targets the extraction model (NER or joint extraction F1 [AA07, AA23, AA25]) rather than the graph itself. The diabetic nephropathy causal KG is the exception: completeness and accuracy are measured through downstream diagnosis on 1,427 inpatients and an expert review of sampled triples [AA02].

Almost no dataset recurs across papers. The 43 rows span 59 dataset families, and only Wikidata appears in more than one paper [AA01, AA20]. Standard benchmarks appear only as secondary transfer or validation tests next to a domain KG: NYT [AA07], DBpedia50k and FB15k-237 [AA09], SQuAD and HotpotQA [AA12], WebQSP, 2WikiMultiHopQA and Mintaka [AA20], KgCLUE [AA25].

Evaluation data are increasingly generated by LLMs or templates. Questions for the internal manufacturing dataset are mainly LLM-generated with expert-checked subsamples [AA12]; MAKES-QA uses LLM-generated QA pairs and LLM-as-a-judge triple scoring [AA30]; Co-MedGraphRAG answers are scored by GPT-4o [AA04]; the costume KGQA questions are template-generated from the KG itself [AA25]; ICSThreatQA questions were partly produced by agents and verified by four experts [AA19].

Released resources exist but availability statements are inconsistent. Releases are printed for QALD-9-plus [AA01], the KEGG_MED data and models [AA11], lecture KG artifacts [AA15], TMF-KG with its questions [AA20] and the smart-product design KG [AA24]. ICSThreatQA gives a GitHub link but its data availability statement says "on request" [AA19]; the costume KGQA paper states that no datasets were generated [AA25]; MAKES-QA states that no data was used [AA30].

Category coverage and placement decisions. Batch 23 adds evidence for KG completion in drug discovery [AA11, AA13], aquaculture [AA09], product design [AA24] and maintenance planning [AA29], all placed under KG completion by the C4/C5 rule; GraphRAG papers [AA12, AA20] are placed under KG retrieval and search; literature-KG fusion [AA13] under entity resolution and KG integration; downstream completeness and accuracy evaluation of the causal KG [AA02] under quality assessment; super-node query timing [AA08] under storage and query processing; SWRL-based design-rule derivation [AA28] under KG reasoning. There is no evidence for ontology and typing, KG-to-text generation, maintenance and evolution, KG-supported applications, fairness, visualisation, or KG-grounded evaluation of LLMs. These placements are reviewer decisions.

A batch of author-built domain KGs with no shared resources. All 71 dataset families occur in one paper only; even Wikidata (via KQA Pro [AB20]), Freebase [AB10] and DrugBank [AB16] appear once. 17 of the 28 included papers introduce a new KG (C1 rows), mostly medical or health KGs (SHKG, hepatitis B, MedKGent, Egyptian COVID-19, EMR quadruplet KG) and four traditional Chinese medicine KGs [AB02, AB19, AB21, AB27], plus education, agriculture, cultural heritage, history, tunnel risk, traffic, cybersecurity, urban and scholarly KGs [AB03, AB04, AB12, AB13, AB17, AB18, AB23, AB30, AB31].

Construction quality is checked on small or indirect samples. Precision is estimated from 50 facts per relation [AB01], 100 annotated samples per course [AB04], LLM judges on 1% of abstracts plus 400 abstracts for experts [AB06], or 200 labelled records [AB27]; several papers give no KG-level evaluation or no size at all [AB13, AB19, AB21, AB23, AB31]. Two report extractor results without dataset size or per-class detail [AB13, AB21].

QA test sets are often derived from the KG being tested. Validation questions taken from training samples [AB03], LLM-generated questions from the seed samples [AB04], questions drawn from the KG's own content with author-written SPARQL [AB09], QA pairs generated from KG subgraphs [AB12], template verbalisations [AB14] and augmented sets from about 15 seed queries without a described split [AB20]. Reported accuracies of 81.67% to 98% [AB02, AB09] therefore measure coverage of the authors' own KG rather than generalisation.

Public benchmarks appear only in method papers, with protocol caveats. The Freebase KGQA suite is subsampled to 1,000 questions for three of five sets [AB10]; the printed ICEWS14 split has more test than training facts [AB22]; multimodal KGC tables mix copied and reproduced baselines [AB29]. AB28 shows on Hetionet and BioKG that training setup, hyperparameters, seeds and splits change model rankings, and AB16 removes DDI edges from its DrugBank KG to avoid label leakage; both practices are rare in this batch.

Data access is weak for domain KGs. Data are available only on request in AB09, AB18, AB27 and AB32 and not at all, for commercial reasons, in AB26; AB02's data statement gives only the ethics approval; the KG behind AB32's gains is not identified. Releases are printed for AB03, AB08, AB10, AB20, AB28 and AB29, with code only for AB16 and sample data only for AB30; AB12 prints a dataset link but also says data are available on reasonable request.

Category coverage and placements. C1 (19 rows), C4 (11), C6 (10) and C11 (9) dominate; single rows support C3 (D3FEND–ATT&CK mapping via an artifact ontology [AB23]), C5 (rule-based chain-inference pruning [AB01]) and C8 (multimodal KG-RAG [AB04]). There is no evidence for C2, C7, C9, C10 or C12–C15. Reviewer placements: temporal extrapolation [AB22] and multi-hop path generation [AB08] under C4 by the C4/C5 rule; DDI prediction [AB16] under C11 as in Batch 21; advisor-advisee inference [AB31] under C4; temporally evolving construction [AB06] under C1 rather than C10.

roles.definition: The study introduces, builds, derives, annotates or releases the dataset/KG/benchmark.
Input data or KG the study builds from, retrieves from or links to (source/background/target KG, retrieval source, seed data).
Used to pre-train a model before the task.
Used to train or fine-tune a model for the task.
Used for model selection or hyperparameter tuning (not dataset validation).
Used to evaluate or compare methods, or as a validation reference for outputs.
Statistics, case study, demonstration, running example or other analysis without a method evaluation.
Used in a deployed or illustrative application.

documented_use_roles.version_rule: version stated if dataset_version names a version number, release, dump/snapshot date, edition year, DOI or Zenodo record (citation years excluded); else "version not stated"
documented_use_roles.limitation_split: limitations_and_scope split by its tags: DL -> limitation_dataset, SS -> scope_study, RI -> reviewer_interpretation; qualifiers such as "(authors)" kept; original field unchanged
